title: Change Data Capture (CDC), Logical Replication Internals & Real-Time Event Streaming
goal: Master high-throughput event-driven data streaming and distributed replication in PostgreSQL: architect Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines using the write-ahead log (WAL), configure Logical Decoding output plugins (pgoutput, wal2json), manage Logical Replication slots, publications, and subscriptions, enforce the transactional outbox pattern, control replication origin tracking, and diagnose replication lag and disk bloat runbooks.
recap: In Day 58, we mastered enterprise database security architecture, multi-tenant RLS, column cryptography, and cryptographic audit ledgers. Today in Day 59, we conquer Change Data Capture, logical replication internals, and real-time event streaming pipelines.

parts.title: Write-Ahead Log (WAL) Streaming & Logical Decoding Internals
say: Welcome to Day Fifty-Nine. Today we master one of the most critical backbones of modern real-time data engineering: Change Data Capture (CDC), PostgreSQL Logical Replication internals, and high-throughput event streaming. In distributed enterprise architectures—connecting operational transactional databases to real-time Apache Kafka streams, cloud data lakehouses, and geo-distributed microservices—batch ETL queries are obsolete. Today, we dissect how PostgreSQL extracts streaming mutation events directly from its internal write-ahead log (WAL) with sub-second latency and zero application performance degradation.

At the heart of PostgreSQL data streaming lies the Logical Decoding Subsystem: an internal engine capability that reads physical write-ahead log records and decodes them into logical row-level mutation events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE).

To enable logical decoding, the primary database server must be configured with wal_level = 'logical': instructing PostgreSQL to enrich write-ahead log records with full tuple descriptors, replica identity keys, and column schema metadata.

Physical WAL records are low-level binary diffs indicating page offsets and disk byte mutations. A physical replica simply replays these exact disk page writes byte-for-byte; however, an external event streaming pipeline cannot ingest raw page offsets—it requires logical tuple values (e.g. customer_id = 42, balance = 1500.00).
To convert physical WAL deltas into structured relational tuples, PostgreSQL invokes a specialized internal memory manager: the ReorderBuffer Subsystem.

In a busy transactional database, hundreds of concurrent transactions write interleaved WAL records into the write-ahead log stream simultaneously: transaction A inserts a row, transaction B updates an account, and transaction A inserts a second row before committing.
If the database emitted WAL records as they arrived on disk, downstream consumers would see fragmented, uncommitted, and potentially aborted transaction data!

The ReorderBuffer solves this fundamental problem by buffering interleaved WAL records in memory, organizing them by transaction ID (XID), and holding them in queue until the transaction's COMMIT record appears in the WAL stream.

The instant a transaction commits, the ReorderBuffer flushes all changes associated with that transaction in exact serial order, passing the ordered tuple stream to the Logical Decoding Output Plugin.

PostgreSQL supports multiple logical decoding output plugins: pgoutput (the native high-performance binary protocol used by built-in logical replication), test_decoding (a readable text format used for testing), and wal2json (a JSON-formatting plugin used by cloud streaming tools).
The output plugin serializes the reassembled tuples into target network formats, streaming events to downstream replication consumers over standard PostgreSQL replication connections.

Crucially, if a transaction rolls back, the ReorderBuffer simply discards all buffered records for that transaction, ensuring that uncommitted mutations are never transmitted over the replication stream.

The memory footprint of the ReorderBuffer is governed by logical_decoding_work_mem (defaulting to 64 megabytes): if a massive bulk transaction exceeds this threshold, the ReorderBuffer writes temporary serialized spill files to disk, preserving server stability.

Furthermore, PostgreSQL logical decoding operates without acquiring shared read locks on production tables: streaming events asynchronously from the WAL buffer without interfering with concurrent online transaction processing (OLTP) transactions.
Database architects tune wal_buffers and max_wal_size: ensuring that write-ahead log pipelines accommodate peak transactional burst volumes without generating checkpoint stalls.
Site reliability engineers monitor WAL generation rates: verifying that logical decoding worker processes keep pace with transaction commit frequencies to maintain near-zero replication lag.

In addition to transactional consistency, logical decoding manages DDL schema evolution gracefully across long-lived streaming pipelines. While the WAL captures physical column alterations, logical decoding output plugins utilize internal relation schema caches to ensure that newly added columns with default values or altered data types are serialized correctly without requiring consumer pipeline restarts.

Furthermore, database engineers tune wal_sender_timeout and max_sync_workers_per_subscription to prevent network jitter from severing active replication connections. Calibrating keepalive heartbeat intervals ensures that transient network hiccups do not prematurely terminate decoding processes during peak transactional throughput periods.
Mastering write-ahead log streaming and ReorderBuffer internals establishes the foundation for high-throughput enterprise event replication.
We now explore how PostgreSQL orchestrates native distributed synchronization using Publications and Subscriptions.
parts.example: Imagine a court stenographer recording testimony in a high-profile legal trial. The stenographer does not wait for a witness to finish speaking before writing; their fingers record every spoken phoneme onto paper ticker tape in real time (physical write-ahead log). Later, an automated transcription software translates the shorthand phonetic symbols into readable legal paragraphs (logical decoding), distributing certified transcripts to legal teams across the country simultaneously.

parts.title: Logical Replication Slots, Publications & Subscriptions
say: While logical decoding provides the event transformation engine, PostgreSQL coordinates distributed synchronization using two complementary primitives: Publications and Subscriptions.
Introduced in PostgreSQL 10 as native logical replication, Publications act as the publisher interface while Subscriptions act as the subscriber interface.

On the publisher database, an administrator creates a Publication using: CREATE PUBLICATION my_pub FOR ALL TABLES; or scopes replication to specific tables: CREATE PUBLICATION orders_pub FOR TABLE orders, line_items;.

In modern PostgreSQL versions, publications support Row Filtering and Column Projection: allowing publishers to replicate only specific rows matching a WHERE clause: CREATE PUBLICATION active_orders FOR TABLE orders WHERE (status = 'ACTIVE'); and specific column lists, preventing sensitive or irrelevant columns from traveling across the network.
On the subscriber database, the administrator creates a Subscription: CREATE SUBSCRIPTION my_sub CONNECTION 'host=primary_db ...' PUBLICATION my_pub;.
When a subscription is created, the subscriber connects to the publisher and creates two critical resources: a Logical Replication Slot and a background Apply Worker process.

First, examine the Logical Replication Slot: the replication slot acts as a guaranteed checkpoint anchor on the publisher's write-ahead log. It tracks the exact Log Sequence Number (LSN) that the subscriber has confirmed receiving and flushing to its local storage.

As long as a replication slot exists, PostgreSQL guarantees that WAL segments newer than the confirmed LSN will never be deleted or recycled by checkpoints, ensuring zero data loss even if the subscriber goes offline for hours during maintenance!

Second, examine the Apply Worker: the apply worker runs as a dedicated background process on the subscriber database, connecting to the publisher slot, streaming incoming binary tuple deltas via the pgoutput plugin, and executing them as standard DML operations locally.

During initial setup, the apply worker triggers Initial Table Synchronization: taking a consistent snapshot of the published tables, copying the existing dataset to the subscriber via COPY commands, and subsequently applying incremental WAL changes until the subscriber catches up to real-time replication.

A vital operational advantage of logical replication over physical streaming replication is Cross-Version and Selective Replication: because logical replication operates on row-level DML rather than physical page blocks, a PostgreSQL 14 publisher can replicate to a PostgreSQL 16 subscriber, enabling seamless Zero-Downtime Major Version Upgrades!

Furthermore, subscribers can maintain additional local indexes, partitions, or summary triggers that do not exist on the publisher, allowing organizations to build dedicated analytical reporting replicas optimized for heavy BI queries.

However, logical replication has explicit boundaries: by default, it does not replicate DDL schema alterations (CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE), sequence values, or large objects, requiring schema migrations to be coordinated across clusters.

To replicate UPDATE and DELETE operations, published tables must define a Replica Identity: defaulting to the table's Primary Key. If a table lacks a primary key, administrators must set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, which forces PostgreSQL to record full row images in the WAL, increasing write amplification.
Database architects monitor subscriber apply worker concurrency: configuring max_sync_workers_per_subscription and max_logical_replication_workers to optimize parallel initial data synchronization.
Site reliability engineers maintain health telemetry on replication slots: auditing slot activity to ensure that downstream network disconnects do not cause publisher disk capacity saturation.

In addition to table-level publications, modern PostgreSQL supports Schema-Level Publications using CREATE PUBLICATION api_pub FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA app_data. This capability automatically includes any newly created tables within the designated schema into the replication stream, eliminating manual publication maintenance during continuous application deployments.

Furthermore, when synchronizing large multi-terabyte tables, reliability engineers monitor the copy phase of initial synchronization. The apply worker initiates parallel worker threads to stream table partitions concurrently, utilizing streaming COPY protocols to saturate available network bandwidth and shorten initial synchronization windows from days down to a few hours.
Mastering publications, subscriptions, and replication slots empowers engineers to architect highly resilient, decoupled database topologies.
We now examine how Change Data Capture pipelines integrate PostgreSQL with Apache Kafka and cloud data lakehouses.
parts.example: Imagine a national news wire syndication service distributing breaking news bulletins to regional newspapers. The national wire establishes specialized topic channels—such as international finance, sports, and science—acting as publications. Regional newspapers subscribe to specific topics of interest, automatically receiving wire dispatches via satellite connections (logical replication slots) the instant a journalist commits a story.

parts.title: CDC Integration Architectures & Event Streaming Pipelines
say: In modern cloud-native architectures, Change Data Capture (CDC) extends beyond database-to-database replication into Enterprise Event Streaming across Kafka, Apache Flink, and cloud data warehouses.

A foundational architectural requirement in distributed microservices is the Transactional Outbox Pattern: guaranteeing that database state mutations and corresponding message broker events succeed or fail as a single atomic unit.

In distributed systems, a notorious failure mode is the Dual-Write Problem: an application service updates a database table (e.g. inserting an order) and subsequently attempts to publish an event to Apache Kafka. If the database transaction commits successfully but the network connection to Kafka fails, the event is lost forever; conversely, if the event publishes but the database transaction rolls back, external systems act on ghost data!

The Transactional Outbox Pattern completely eliminates dual-write anomalies by leveraging ACID guarantees: the application writes both the operational business entity and an event record into an outbox table within the identical database transaction: INSERT INTO orders ...; INSERT INTO outbox_events ...; COMMIT;.
Because both operations reside in the same atomic transaction, either both succeed or both fail: zero partial failure states can ever exist.
To publish outbox events to external message brokers, distributed architectures deploy Debezium: an open-source distributed CDC platform built on top of Kafka Connect.
Debezium connects directly to PostgreSQL as a logical replication client: attaching to a dedicated logical replication slot and tailing the write-ahead log in real time.

The instant the outbox transaction commits, Debezium decodes the outbox table mutation from the WAL stream, transforms the payload into a structured JSON or Apache Avro message, and publishes it to the appropriate Apache Kafka topic with guaranteed at-least-once delivery.

A profound operational benefit of log-based CDC over polling-based CDC (such as SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE status = 'PENDING') is Zero Read Overhead: Debezium does not execute any SQL queries against the database tables, completely eliminating polling table locks and index scan overhead on production database servers.

Furthermore, log-based CDC captures every single intermediate state change: if an account balance is updated five times within a single second, log-based CDC streams all five distinct events in exact chronological sequence, whereas polling queries only observe the final snapshot value.

Downstream consumers—such as Apache Flink streaming analytics engines, Elasticsearch full-text search indexes, and Apache Iceberg data lakehouses—consume the CDC event stream to maintain synchronized, real-time materialized views.

To optimize event serialization throughput, enterprise architectures utilize Schema Registry and Apache Avro: validating event schemas against registered contracts and reducing binary payload sizes by up to seventy percent compared to verbose JSON strings.

Database architects configure outbox table truncation policies: utilizing automated background vacuuming or partitioning outbox tables by day to drop expired event partitions without incurring expensive DELETE statement overhead.

Site reliability engineers maintain end-to-end monitoring from PostgreSQL WAL generation to Kafka consumer group lag: ensuring that event delivery latencies remain under two hundred milliseconds across global production regions.

In addition to Debezium connectors, enterprise data lakehouse architectures deploy real-time CDC consumers using Apache Flink and Apache Spark Streaming. These stream processing engines consume Kafka CDC changelogs, deduplicate unordered events using monotonic event sequence numbers, and apply merge-on-read operations directly against Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake storage tables.

Furthermore, to guarantee event idempotency across downstream distributed microservices, application architectures inject unique UUID idempotency keys into the outbox event payload. Downstream consumers maintain an idempotent event ledger or Redis cache, discarding duplicate event deliveries that may occur during network retries or Kafka consumer rebalancing.

To optimize outbox table maintenance, database architects implement automated partition dropping using pg_partman. By creating daily or hourly outbox partitions, the platform drops processed event partitions instantaneously using DROP TABLE, avoiding the heavy write-amplification and table bloat associated with bulk DELETE statements.
Mastering CDC integration architectures and the transactional outbox pattern bridges the gap between relational persistence and real-time distributed microservices.
We now examine multi-master replication conflicts and replication origin management.
parts.example: Imagine a municipal postal dispatch center processing registered parcel shipments. If a postal clerk updates the parcel status in a computer terminal but forgets to print the physical routing barcode label, the package becomes lost in transit (dual-write partial failure). Under the transactional outbox pattern, the computer prints the routing label inside the identical transaction that records the parcel acceptance, ensuring physical parcels and digital tracking numbers remain in perfect lockstep.

parts.title: Replication Conflicts, Replication Origins & Multi-Master Geodistribution
say: When deploying multi-region or active-active distributed databases, database engineers confront one of distributed computing greatest hurdles: Replication Conflicts and Multi-Master Synchronization.

In an active-active replication topology where two database nodes (e.g., US-East and EU-West) accept write transactions concurrently, both nodes may attempt to update the same customer record simultaneously.

Because changes propagate asynchronously across the trans-Atlantic network, network latency creates a race condition: Node A and Node B commit conflicting updates locally before receiving each other's replication streams.

When the apply worker on Node B attempts to replay the change originated on Node A, a Replication Conflict occurs: for example, a duplicate key violation if both nodes inserted a row with the same primary key, or an update-missing-row conflict if Node B deleted a record that Node A modified.

In default native logical replication, encountering any replication conflict causes the Apply Worker to halt immediately with an error, freezing replication on that subscription until an administrator manually resolves the conflict!

To build resilient multi-master and bi-directional replication topologies, database architects deploy Replication Origin Tracking via PostgreSQL native origin functions: pg_replication_origin_create, pg_replication_origin_setup, and pg_replication_origin_advance.

The most insidious danger in bi-directional replication is the Circular Replication Echo Loop: Node A replicates a change to Node B; Node B applies the change, generating a new WAL record; Node B's publisher sees the new WAL record and replicates it back to Node A; Node A applies it again, triggering an infinite ping-pong replication loop that saturates network and CPU capacity!

Replication origins eliminate circular echo loops: when Node B's apply worker replays an incoming change, it tags the active session with the origin ID of Node A. Node B's publication filters out any WAL record whose origin matches Node A, preventing the change from echoing back across the wire.
Furthermore, modern enterprise replication engines implement Automated Conflict Resolution Policies: such as Last-Write-Wins (LWW) based on monotonic commit timestamps.

In a Last-Write-Wins strategy, every table includes an updated_at timestamp generated using synchronized NTP clocks or TrueTime hardware. When a conflict occurs, the apply worker compares the incoming timestamp with the local row timestamp: if the incoming update is newer, it overwrites the local row; if older, the incoming change is discarded.

For financial accounts and counter metrics where overwriting causes data loss, architectures utilize Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs): representing balances as delta increments (+50, -20) rather than absolute values, ensuring that operations commute mathematically regardless of arrival order.
Database teams establish automated conflict logging tables: capturing discarded updates and logging conflict metrics to observability dashboards for forensic audit review.
Site reliability engineers maintain health alerts on apply worker status: detecting conflict halts in non-CRDT tables before replication lag accumulates.

In addition to timestamp-based resolution, enterprise active-active architectures implement Column-Level Conflict Resolution. Rather than overwriting an entire row when a concurrent update occurs, the custom conflict handler compares updated column sets: if Node A modified customer email while Node B modified shipping address, the engine merges both field updates cleanly into the target record without data loss.

Furthermore, distributed database platforms implement Conflict Notification Webhooks. When an unresolvable data collision occurs—such as two conflicting withdrawals that exceed a shared account credit limit—the replication engine isolates the conflicting payload into an exception table and dispatches an automated alert to financial operations teams for manual reconciliation.

To maintain deterministic causal ordering across geographically separated data centers, database engineers deploy Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC). By combining physical NTP clock readings with monotonic logical counters, Hybrid Logical Clocks guarantee that causally dependent transactions are evaluated in correct chronological sequence across distributed nodes.

Finally, site reliability engineers establish automated chaos engineering drills: simulating cross-region network partitions to verify that replication origins prevent circular loops and that catch-up synchronization resumes seamlessly once network connectivity is restored.
Mastering replication origins and conflict resolution policies transforms fragile point-to-point replication links into robust, fault-tolerant global data meshes.
We now examine replication lag telemetry, slot health forensics, and disk overflow prevention runbooks.
parts.example: Imagine two international currency trading desks in London and Tokyo updating a corporate treasury ledger simultaneously. If the London desk purchases Euros while the Tokyo desk sells Yen against the same account without coordination, conflicting ledger entries collide. By establishing strict replication origin timestamps and automated conflict reconciliation rules, the global treasury system merges both transactions deterministically without financial discrepancies.

parts.title: Diagnostic Forensics, EXPLAIN Telemetry & Replication Lag Monitoring Runbooks
say: To conclude Day Fifty-Nine, we examine production diagnostic forensics, EXPLAIN telemetry, and replication lag monitoring runbooks: preventing replication slot disk bloat and maintaining sub-second streaming throughput.
In high-throughput enterprise databases, the number one operational risk associated with logical replication is Inactive Replication Slot Disk Exhaustion.

Recall that a replication slot instructs PostgreSQL to retain all WAL segments from the subscriber's confirmed flush LSN. If an external consumer (such as a Debezium connector or reporting replica) crashes or experiences a network partition, the slot becomes Inactive: active = FALSE in pg_replication_slots.

While the consumer is offline, the publisher continues processing write transactions, generating gigabytes of new write-ahead log files. Because the inactive slot holds the retention checkpoint, PostgreSQL cannot recycle or delete old WAL segments!

Within hours, the accumulated WAL segments fill the publisher's disk volume: when disk utilization reaches one hundred percent, the PostgreSQL primary server enters emergency panic shutdown, crashing production availability across the entire enterprise!

To permanently eliminate disk exhaustion from orphaned replication slots, modern PostgreSQL implements the max_slot_wal_keep_size configuration directive: setting a hard upper boundary (e.g. 50GB or 100GB) on the maximum volume of WAL that replication slots are permitted to retain.

If an inactive slot falls behind and unconsumed WAL exceeds max_slot_wal_keep_size, PostgreSQL automatically Invalidates the slot (wal_status = 'lost') and resumes normal WAL recycling, preserving primary database availability at the expense of requiring the downstream consumer to perform a fresh snapshot resync.
To monitor real-time replication health, reliability engineers inspect the pg_stat_replication system view: tracking write_lag, flush_lag, and replay_lag.

Write lag measures the time elapsed between writing a WAL record on the primary and the subscriber writing it to disk; flush lag measures the time until the subscriber flushes the record to persistent storage; and replay lag measures the time until the apply worker successfully commits the change locally.

In healthy production pipelines, all three lag metrics remain under one second: if replay_lag spikes while write_lag remains low, the diagnosis is clear: the subscriber's apply worker is CPU-bound or contending for local table write locks.

Furthermore, database administrators monitor ReorderBuffer memory consumption via pg_stat_database temp_bytes: detecting large bulk transactions that spill intermediate decoding files to disk and increasing logical_decoding_work_mem to restore high-speed in-memory decoding.

SREs maintain automated alerting runbooks: firing high-priority alerts whenever pg_replication_slots active = FALSE for more than ten minutes or when replication lag exceeds five gigabytes of WAL bytes.

Finally, production runbooks mandate documenting replication topologies, publication contracts, and slot retention policies in central engineering repositories: ensuring seamless operational failovers across cloud regions.

In addition to slot capacity monitoring, reliability engineers track write-ahead log generation velocity using Prometheus node exporters and pg_stat_wal. By establishing baseline metrics for hourly WAL generation rates, monitoring systems can detect runaway application transactions or un-indexed batch updates that generate abnormal WAL spikes before they saturate replication slots.

Furthermore, database administrators implement automated failover runbooks for logical replication subscribers. When promoting a standby replica during a regional disaster recovery event, the orchestration system re-points existing subscriptions to the newly promoted primary database using ALTER SUBSCRIPTION my_sub CONNECTION refresh publication, resuming event consumption without re-syncing data.

To protect network bandwidth across inter-region replication topologies, enterprise architectures enable wire-level network compression on replication connections. By compressing pgoutput binary streams using LZ4 or Zstandard algorithms, organizations reduce cross-region data transfer egress costs and minimize network transmission latency.

Finally, production runbooks mandate documenting all publication contracts, replication slot ownership, and consumer failover procedures in central architecture wikis: ensuring uninterrupted operational excellence across the entire enterprise data platform.
Mastering replication lag forensics, slot capacity guardrails, and telemetry monitoring guarantees that enterprise event streaming pipelines operate with bulletproof reliability.
Congratulations on completing Day Fifty-Nine: you now wield complete command over Change Data Capture, PostgreSQL logical replication, and distributed event streaming.
parts.example: Imagine a municipal water reservoir receiving mountain snowmelt runoff through a master intake canal. If downstream irrigation gates are closed for maintenance but the upstream intake canal remains wide open, water accumulates rapidly until the reservoir overflows its retention dams. In PostgreSQL, an inactive replication slot blocks WAL recycling like a closed irrigation gate, causing write-ahead logs to accumulate until local server disks are completely exhausted.

-- Establishing Replication Monitoring Runbooks: Diagnostic Metrics, Operational Dangers, and Remediations
CREATE TABLE replication_monitoring_runbook (
    diagnostic_monitoring_metric TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    telemetry_view_source TEXT,
    operational_threshold_danger TEXT,
    performance_remediation_action TEXT,
    system_availability_impact TEXT
);
INSERT INTO replication_monitoring_runbook VALUES
('Replication Slot Lag Bytes', 'pg_replication_slots (wal_status, active)', 'Slot inactive while WAL exceeds max_slot_wal_keep_size', 'Drop or invalidate orphaned slot; resume consumer worker', 'Prevents primary server disk exhaustion and database crash'),
('Apply Worker Network Delay', 'pg_stat_replication (write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag)', 'Replay lag exceeds 60 seconds on read replica', 'Increase logical apply worker parallelism or network bandwidth', 'Ensures read replicas maintain real-time reporting freshness'),
('ReorderBuffer Disk Spill', 'pg_stat_database temp_bytes and log warnings', 'Large transactions spill ReorderBuffer slices to disk', 'Increase logical_decoding_work_mem from 64MB to 256MB', 'Eliminates temporary disk I/O; accelerates decoding throughput');

SELECT 
    diagnostic_monitoring_metric,
    telemetry_view_source,
    operational_threshold_danger,
    system_availability_impact
FROM replication_monitoring_runbook
ORDER BY diagnostic_monitoring_metric;

check.question: What critical operational safeguard prevents inactive replication slots from filling server storage disks and causing primary database crashes?
options: Configuring 'max_slot_wal_keep_size' to enforce a hard maximum limit on retained WAL volume, invalidating lagging slots if exceeded
Disabling all transaction commits on the primary database
Rebooting the server every thirty minutes automatically
Truncating all customer tables when disk space reaches ninety percent
check.why: max_slot_wal_keep_size sets a hard ceiling on retained WAL, invalidating lagging slots to protect primary server disk availability.

summary: Logical decoding reads physical WAL records and reassembles committed transactions via the ReorderBuffer in memory.
Publications publish row changes via pgoutput; Subscriptions consume streams using Apply Workers and Replication Slots.
The Transactional Outbox Pattern writes entity mutations and outbox events in a single ACID transaction, eliminating dual-write bugs.
Replication Origins (pg_replication_origin) identify mutation sources, preventing circular echo loops in active-active topologies.
max_slot_wal_keep_size enforces hard limits on retained WAL, preventing inactive replication slots from causing disk exhaustion crashes.

projectStep.title: Enterprise Real-Time Event Streaming & Logical Replication Pipeline
steps: Configure PostgreSQL logical decoding with wal_level = logical and calibrate logical_decoding_work_mem buffer sizes.
Architect selective publications with row filters and column projections to minimize replication network overhead.
Deploy the Transactional Outbox Pattern with Debezium to stream atomic event notifications to Apache Kafka topics.
Implement replication origin tracking (pg_replication_origin) to prevent circular loop echoes in active-active multi-region clusters.
Establish replication lag monitoring using pg_stat_replication and configure max_slot_wal_keep_size to eliminate disk bloat.
